summary: Mometasone furoate 0.1% cream is a medium-potency topical corticosteroid for the inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses in patients 2 years and older. Applied as a thin film once daily, it acts locally with anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive effects; systemic absorption can cause HPA-axis suppression when used over large areas or under occlusion.
indications: Relief of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses (e.g. atopic dermatitis, psoriasis) in patients 2 years of age or older

dosage.d: Apply a thin film of 0.1% cream to affected skin once daily
dosage.t: Discontinue when control achieved; reassess diagnosis if no improvement within 2 weeks
dosage.n: May be used in children 2 years and older; not recommended below 2 years; safety beyond 3 weeks in children not established

admin: Apply a thin film to affected skin areas once daily
For topical use only; not for oral, ophthalmic, or intravaginal use
Avoid use on the face, groin, or axillae unless directed
Do not use under occlusive dressings unless directed by a physician
Do not apply in the diaper area in patients still in diapers or plastic pants (these act as occlusion)
moa: Like other topical corticosteroids, mometasone furoate has anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive properties. It is thought to induce phospholipase A2-inhibitory proteins (lipocortins) that suppress release of arachidonic acid, thereby reducing biosynthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes.

absolute: History of hypersensitivity to mometasone furoate or any component of the preparation
relative: Application over large surface areas or under occlusion (systemic absorption risk)
Untreated skin infection at the site
Use on face, groin, or axillae
Use longer than 3 weeks in children
monitor: Evaluate periodically for HPA-axis suppression with large surface area or occlusive use
Refer to ophthalmology if visual symptoms (cataract/glaucoma risk) occur

preg: Pregnancy Category C. No adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; corticosteroids are teratogenic in animals (including after dermal application). Use during pregnancy only if potential benefit justifies potential risk; apply to the smallest area for the shortest duration.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk; it is unknown whether topical use yields detectable amounts in milk. Use caution when administering to a nursing woman; avoid application to the breast/nipple before nursing.
renal: No specific dose adjustment for topical use; systemic exposure is minimal at recommended dosing.
hepatic: Use caution; liver failure is a predisposing factor for HPA-axis suppression from systemic absorption.

minor: Other topical or systemic corticosteroids (additive systemic corticosteroid exposure)
interactions.diagnostics: May lower adrenal corticosteroid secretion; can affect Cortrosyn (ACTH-stimulation) testing with extensive use

emergency: Symptomatic adrenal crisis after abrupt withdrawal of prolonged therapy

monitoring: Signs of HPA-axis suppression (especially with large area, occlusion, prolonged use, or in children)
Local skin reactions: atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, infection
Visual symptoms suggestive of cataract or glaucoma
Treatment response and reassessment of diagnosis if no improvement within 2 weeks
Growth in pediatric patients with prolonged use
counsel: Use exactly as directed; for external skin use only
Do not apply to the face, underarms, or groin unless told to
Do not bandage or cover treated skin so as to be occlusive unless directed
Do not use to treat diaper rash or apply in the diaper area
Report any visual symptoms or local reactions to your provider
Stop and contact your provider if no improvement within 2 weeks
Do not use other corticosteroid products together without consulting your provider
pearls: Medium-potency topical steroid; once-daily dosing aids adherence versus other agents.
About 0.4% of an applied dose enters circulation after 8 hours on intact, non-occluded skin; absorption rises with inflammation, occlusion, large area, or broken skin.
Children have a higher skin-surface-to-body-mass ratio and greater risk of HPA-axis suppression and Cushing's syndrome; HPA suppression occurred in ~16% of infants treated ~3 weeks over large areas.
Mometasone furoate also exists as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis and as an inhaled formulation for asthma; doses and indications differ from this topical cream and should not be interchanged.
Discontinue when control is achieved and avoid prolonged continuous use to limit local and systemic adverse effects.
missed: If a once-daily application is missed, apply it when remembered; if it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed application and resume the usual schedule. Do not apply extra cream to make up a missed dose.
overdose: Topically applied mometasone furoate can be absorbed in amounts sufficient to produce systemic corticosteroid effects (e.g., HPA-axis suppression). Chronic overuse may cause Cushingoid features and hyperglycemia. Management is symptomatic and supportive with gradual withdrawal; avoid abrupt cessation after prolonged extensive use to prevent adrenal insufficiency.
